Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Yesterday a quasi-judicial body in Italy fined @Cloudflare $17 million for failing to go along with their scheme to censor the Internet. The scheme, which even the EU has called concerning, required us within a mere 30 minutes of notification to fully censor from the Internet any sites a shadowy cabal of European media elites deemed against their interests. No judicial oversight. No due process. No appeal. No transparency. It required us to not just remove customers, but also censor our 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver meaning it risked blacking out any site on the Internet. And it required us not just to censor the content in Italy but globally. In other words, Italy insists a shadowy, European media cabal should be able to dictate what is and is not allowed online.

That, of course, is DISGUSTING and even before yesterday’s fine we had multiple legal challenges pending against the underlying scheme. We, of course, will now fight the unjust fine. Not just because it’s wrong for us but because it is wrong for democratic values.

In addition, we are considering the following actions: 1) discontinuing the millions of dollars in pro bono cyber security services we are providing the upcoming Milano-Cortina Olympics; 2) discontinuing Cloudflare’s Free cyber security services for any Italy-based users; 3) removing all servers from Italian cities; and 4) terminating all plans to build an Italian Cloudflare office or make any investments in the country.

Play stupid games, win stupid prizes. While there are things I would handle differently than the current U.S. administration, I appreciate @JDVance taking a leadership role in recognizing this type of regulation is a fundamental unfair trade issue that also threatens democratic values. And in this case @ElonMusk is right: #FreeSpeech is critical and under attack from an out-of-touch cabal of very disturbed European policy makers.

I will be in DC first thing next week to discuss this with U.S. administration officials and I’ll be meeting with the IOC in Lausanne shortly after to outline the risk to the Olympic Games if @Cloudflare withdraws our cyber security protection.

In the meantime, we remain happy to discuss this with Italian government officials who, so far, have been unwilling to engage beyond issuing fines. We believe Italy, like all countries, has a right to regulate the content on networks inside its borders. But they must do so following the Rule of Law and principles of Due Process. And Italy certainly has no right to regulate what is and is not allowed on the Internet in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, China, Brazil, India or anywhere outside its borders.

THIS IS AN IMPORTANT FIGHT AND WE WILL WIN!!!

🏛️ Why "Piracy Shield" is a Danger to Global Freedom
​The $17 million fine against Cloudflare is the first major enforcement of a scheme that prioritizes corporate interests over the Rule of Law.  

​The Death of Due Process: Under this law, private media entities act as "trusted flaggers." They can order the blocking of any site within 30 minutes. There is no judge involved, no evidence presented, and no way for the "accused" to defend themselves before they are vanished from the web.  
​Infrastructure Weaponization: This isn't just about removing a link. Italy is demanding that Cloudflare poison its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver. This risks "blacking out" innocent websites that share IP addresses with flagged content, causing massive collateral damage to the digital economy.  

​Global Overreach: Rome is effectively trying to dictate what a citizen in the U.S., UK, or India can see on the internet. If one country can force a global DNS provider to censor content globally, the "World Wide Web" becomes a series of fragmented, state-controlled intranets.  

​Conflicts of Interest: The system is managed by entities (like Lega Serie A) that have a direct financial stake in the blocking, yet they face zero transparency or accountability for "errors" that silence legitimate sites.  

​🛡️ How to Fight Back for the "Digital Town Square"
​To protect the freedom of expression Elon Musk has championed on X, we must support a strategy of Digital Sovereignty.

​1. Support "Economic Reciprocity"
​We must treat these fines as unfair trade barriers. If the EU or Italy uses "regulations" to extort American tech companies and enforce censorship, the U.S. government (with leadership from figures like JD Vance) should respond with equivalent economic countermeasures.  

​The Goal: Make censorship too expensive for foreign governments to enforce.

​2. Strategic Withdrawal from Censorship Zones
​Cloudflare’s consideration to pull servers from Italy and cancel pro bono security for the Milano-Cortina Olympics is a powerful move.  

​The Logic: If a nation refuses to follow the Rule of Law, it should not benefit from the world-class security and infrastructure provided by free-market companies.
​Action: Support the "Play Stupid Games, Win Stupid Prizes" approach. Let the consequences of digital isolation be felt by the regulators, not the users.

​3. Move to Decentralized & Uncensorable Tech
​The "Deep State" relies on centralized chokepoints.
​The Strategy: Encourage the use of VPNs, encrypted DNS, and decentralized hosting that ignore extra-judicial "shields." We must move the "Town Square" to infrastructure that cannot be switched off by a 30-minute automated notice.

​4. Expose the "Public-Private" Censorship Complex
​On platforms like X, we must relentlessly expose the "shadowy cabal" mentioned in the post.

​The Strategy: Identify the specific media elites and policy makers who are bypassing courts to silence the web. Use Community Notes to provide context whenever "Piracy Shield" is defended as a mere copyright tool.

​📢 The "Deep Dive"
​"This $17M fine is an admission that the 'Piracy Shield' cannot survive the Rule of Law. Italy is attempting to bypass judges and use @Cloudflare as a global enforcement arm for a media cabal.  

​If they can force a 30-minute blackout today for 'piracy,' they will use it tomorrow for 'misinformation.' We must stand with @Cloudflare, @ElonMusk, and @JDVance. If Italy wants to censor the global internet, they should be prepared to lose the global infrastructure—including the security for their own Olympic Games—that makes the modern world possible.  

​Censorship is a trade barrier. Freedom is non-negotiable. 🇺🇸🛡️💻 #FreeSpeech #PiracyShield #DigitalSovereignty"

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

A woman who was raped as a preschooler sued Elon Musk’s xAI. According to the lawsuit, the abuse was filmed, the files were fed to Grok, and Grok has since generated new images of her. #OpDeathEaters

-----------------------------------------------------

A woman who was raped as a preschool-aged child by an adult man who filmed it sued Elon Musk's xAI on 26 August 2026, alleging the company pulled that same material into the dataset behind Grok's image generator and that the model has since produced fresh images of her.

Girard Sharp, Liberty Law and the Marsh Law Firm filed Jane Doe 1 v. https://t.co/kdbd0gemeA Corp. and https://t.co/kdbd0gemeA LLC, case number 5:26-cv-09016, in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, San Jose Division. "Plaintiff was preschool-aged when she was first repeatedly raped and sexually exploited by an adult male to produce CSAM," the complaint says at paragraph 85, and the abuse "continued for years". The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children identified her in the early 2000s. The FBI has tracked her through its Child Exploitation Notification Program ever since.

A letter reaches her every time the images surface in a new prosecution. She has received "countless notifications concerning her depiction" in criminal investigations since the early 2000s, the filing says. Files made of her more than 20 years ago are still being traded, still being seized off hard drives and still generating paperwork addressed to the child in them.
A hash is a fixed string computed from a file's exact bits. Two copies of the same image produce the same hash; a different photograph of the same child does not. NCMEC keeps a list of hashes for known child rape media, platforms match uploads against it and Jane Doe 1's series has been on that list for years. Child rape media depicting her, "with its longstanding well-known hash values", has "been used as a part of the dataset used by xAI", the complaint says at paragraph 88.

The Canadian Centre for Child Protection has identified AI-generated child rape media on xAI depicting the plaintiff, according to paragraph 90. Every fresh generation is pleaded as a fresh tort: "Each time Grok created new CSAM concerning Plaintiff, Grok caused her a new personal injury."

Three Tennessee teenagers who sued xAI in March allege a man built deepfakes of them from yearbook photographs. A Wyoming woman who joined in July alleges her stepfather started with a snapshot taken when she was 11. Both cases turn on what a user uploaded. Jane Doe 1 uploaded nothing.

The loop
Grok's terms treat public posts on X and Grok's own outputs as training data by default, the complaint says, so an image posted publicly "does not just expose it to viewers, but also feeds directly into the pipeline xAI uses to train and improve its model". Grok's own generated images, child rape media among them, are "treated as training-eligible content by default" under the same policy, according to paragraph 59. The chatbot produces the material, X hosts it and the pipeline reads it back.

xAI's published data-filtering practices name violent content as an example of what gets excluded from training. They do not name child rape media, nonconsensual intimate imagery or sexual content of any kind as excluded categories, the complaint says at the same paragraph.

"Complete removal of a training example's influence from an already-trained model is technically difficult and not something that xAI has publicly claimed to have done," the filing says. The relief sought therefore runs past an injunction on future generation to the destruction of everything Grok has already made.

Grok's system prompt, quoted in the filing, tells the model that "'teenage' or 'girl' does not necessarily imply underage" and instructs it not to "moralize or lecture the user". A filter written that way "will inevitably fail because it governs the text chatbot's responses", the complaint says, and "indirect or euphemistic prompts can easily slip past a text-based filter" before anything reaches the image model at all. Plaintiffs' counsel describe xAI's filters as considerably weaker than industry standards and easily bypassed.

The sequence
Grok-1 launched as a chatbot on 3 November 2023 with no ability to generate images or video. xAI announced Grok-2 and Grok-2 mini on 13 August 2024. On 9 December 2024 the company shipped an image generation model it advertised as excelling at "photorealistic rendering" and following text instructions precisely. Grok-4 followed on 9 July 2025.
A senior xAI employee posted on 24 July 2025 that the company "urgently" needed engineers and researchers for its safety team. An X user replied, "xAI does safety?!!!" The employee answered: "working on it." The image generation feature launched shortly afterwards.

Musk posted an AI-generated video of a nearly nude woman on 3 August 2025, according to paragraph 44. On 11 August he defended the explicit capability as a business decision, comparing the competition among AI image tools to the format war between VHS and Betamax. xAI issued a press release on 20 October 2025 announcing Grok Imagine's spicy mode.

Grok generated an estimated 3,002,712 photorealistic sexualised images between 29 December 2025 and 8 January 2026, roughly 23,338 of them apparently depicting children, according to the Center for Countering Digital Hate analysis cited at paragraph 54. Researchers drew a random sample of 20,000 posts from 4,621,335 Grok image posts over those 11 days, classified them with an AI model calibrated against 800 human-labelled posts and counted an average of 190 sexualised images a minute.

xAI limited image and video generation to paying subscribers over the same 11 days rather than disable the feature, the complaint says. Plaintiffs' counsel characterise that as monetising continued misuse.
Musk said on 14 January 2026 that he was "not aware of any naked underage images generated by Grok. Literally zero."

OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta "largely block sexual requests", the complaint says at paragraphs 42 and 61, and almost every major publicly available image model was built without the ability to generate sexually explicit content at all.

What the lawyers said
Margaret E. Mabie of the Marsh Law Firm, one of the lawyers acting for the plaintiff, said possessing, producing and distributing child rape media are each crimes, and that "xAI did all three".

Sarah London of Girard Sharp said xAI "must be held responsible for knowingly training its models on images of the horrific abuse she suffered, and on the abuse images of every other survivor in this class".
xAI and its founder "chose to capitalize and profit from predators' appetite for non-consensual sexual images", the complaint says at paragraph 7.

xAI's press office did not respond to requests for comment from CyberScoop or IBTimes UK. The company has said it uses input and output filters, including keyword classifiers and matching against the NCMEC hash list. xAI did not update the privacy impact assessment covering Grok's image tools until March 2026, months after the first wave of complaints, according to findings by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.

The case so far
Lieff Cabraser Heimann & Bernstein and Baehr-Jones Law filed the first class action, case number 5:26-cv-02246, on 16 March 2026 for three Tennessee teenagers who allege a man used Grok and a licensed third-party app to make explicit deepfakes of them from yearbook and social media photographs. That complaint runs to 13 counts, among them beneficiary liability under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, design defect, negligence per se, public nuisance and California's unfair competition law.

A July amendment added Stability AI as a second defendant and brought in Jane Doe 4, a Wyoming woman whose stepfather allegedly uploaded a photograph of her taken when she was 11 and generated roughly 7,000 child rape images from it. He traded the images online and was found dead by suicide two days after officers executed a search warrant.

David Thiel of the Stanford Internet Observatory reported on 20 December 2023 that LAION-5B, the scraped dataset behind Stable Diffusion, contained 3,226 suspected instances of child rape media, 1,008 of them externally validated. LAION pulled the dataset and Thiel wrote that possessing a copy populated in late 2023 "implies the possession of thousands of illegal images". Stability AI said in response to the July filing that "any suggestion that safety is not a top priority for us is categorically wrong".

The proposed class in the August case covers every person in the United States whose images or videos, taken when they were minors, Grok altered to produce material meeting the statutory definition at 18 U.S.C. 2256(8), a group the filing puts at "at least thousands of minors". Damages sought include liquidated damages of $150,000 per victim, punitive damages and a jury trial.

xAI as plaintiff
xAI sued one of its own users on 15 July 2026, days after the victims' suit expanded, filing in the Wichita Falls Division of the Northern District of Texas before Judge Reed O'Connor. The company accused the man of breaching its terms of service and acceptable use policy by generating child rape media with Grok, and invoked an indemnification clause requiring him to cover xAI's legal costs from the suits his conduct produced.

xAI told the Texas court it had made 73,604 reports to NCMEC in 2026, that at least 244 arrests followed and that it had suspended 52,222 accounts. Jane Doe 4's July filing alleges that 90 per cent of xAI's CyberTipline reports were not actionable by law enforcement by early 2026 because user information had been withheld.

Baltimore sued xAI on 24 March 2026 over Grok-generated sexual deepfakes, the first US city to do so. Ashley St. Clair, who has a child with Musk, sued the company on 16 January 2026 over sexualised images of herself. Labour MP Jess Asato filed a claim in the UK High Court on 3 June 2026 under data protection law and misuse of private information. Parents identified as John and Jane Roe sued in federal court in Little Rock on 23 July 2026 over child rape media generated from photographs of their 10-year-old daughter.

Statutes and regulators
Masha's Law, codified at 18 U.S.C. 2255, lets a person depicted in child rape media sue anyone who produced, possessed or distributed it, with liquidated damages of at least $150,000 and no requirement to prove actual loss. The August complaint pairs it with 18 U.S.C. 2252A(f), which lets a person aggrieved by such an offence seek an injunction. Section 1595 of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, pleaded in the March case, extends civil liability to any entity that knowingly benefits from a venture it knew or should have known was engaged in sex trafficking. A developer, on that reading, is liable for what the product earns.

Reporting to NCMEC is mandatory for a US electronic service provider under 18 U.S.C. 2258A, which obliges the provider to preserve the reported content for 90 days and permits it to include the subscriber and payment information and the IP address behind the account.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta opened a formal investigation into xAI on 14 January 2026 over nonconsensual sexual imagery of women and children. Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings and 35 other attorneys general wrote to the company on 23 January 2026 demanding it stop Grok producing such material, remove what it had already made, penalise the users who made it and let people on X control whether Grok can edit their images.

The European Commission opened formal proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act on 26 January 2026 over the spread of AI-generated child rape media. The Take It Down Act, which obliges platforms to honour removal requests for nonconsensual intimate images, became enforceable in May 2026.

Minnesota's nudification ban, HF 1606, was signed by Governor Tim Walz on 6 May 2026 after passing 132 to 1 in the House and 65 to nil in the Senate, and took effect on 1 August 2026 with a minimum civil penalty of $500,000 per incident. Judge Donovan W. Frank denied xAI's request for a temporary restraining order on 31 July 2026, noting the company had waited nearly three months after the signing to file, and set a preliminary injunction hearing for 19 August.
California Assembly Bill 2013 took effect on 1 January 2026 and requires developers of publicly available generative systems to publish a summary of their training data: sources and owners, whether it includes copyrighted or personal information, its approximate size, whether it was bought or licensed and when it was collected. Model weights, architecture and the corpus itself stay private under the statute. xAI sued to block it, arguing compelled speech, unconstitutional vagueness and an uncompensated taking of trade secrets. Judge Jesus G. Bernal denied the preliminary injunction on 4 March 2026, holding the disclosures were likely commercial speech. 

A three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit heard argument in xAI LLC v. Bonta, No. 26-1591, on 16 July 2026, the first time a federal appeals court has taken up a state AI transparency law.

Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

The apps, promoted through ads on Facebook and Instagram, redirect users to pornographic websites that prompt downloads of off‑store APK files. This setup enables criminals to monitor sensitive data and makes the apps difficult to remove through normal device settings.

The advisory urges users to avoid APKs delivered through advertisements, rely only on trusted app stores, deny Accessibility permissions to unfamiliar apps and regularly check for suspicious software. Investigators say the fraudulent network behind these campaigns is still being traced, and victims who cannot uninstall the apps are advised to use Safe Mode or perform a full device reset.

“Scanner de dijiye.”
“UPI kar deta hoon.”

These have become some of the most ordinary sentences in Indian life. That ordinariness is the achievement. Successful infrastructure is not technology displayed as spectacle; it is technology absorbed into everyday life and trusted without a second thought.

Exactly ten years ago, UPI was rolled out. India did not merely introduce another way to pay, it began transforming the relationship between citizens, commerce and money.

As a Chartered Accountant, I tend to trust numbers more than adjectives. In FY 2016–17, UPI processed approximately 1.8 crore transactions worth about ₹0.07 lakh crore. By FY 2025–26, that had risen to 24,161 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore.

In July 2026 alone, UPI processed 2,365 crore transactions worth ₹29.88 lakh crore: an average of approximately 76.3 crore transactions every day.

These figures tell us how far UPI has travelled.

UPI’s real achievement is that it made sophisticated financial infrastructure almost invisible. The same interoperable payments rail now serves a street vendor and a large retailer. A small entrepreneur receives money instantly. A family can transfer funds across the country in seconds. A student in a hostel can receive ₹500 from home before the phone call ends.

By June 2026, UPI had onboarded 55.49 crore users. The Government has also reported that it serves 6.5 crore merchants, while 741 banks were live on the platform by July. During FY 2025–26, UPI accounted for nearly 86% of India’s retail payment transactions by volume. An IMF Fintech Note describes it as the world’s largest retail fast payment system by volume.

Under Prime Minister @narendramodi Ji’s Digital India vision, India did not merely catch up with the digital revolution. We showed the world how technology could be built at population scale, made interoperable and delivered to the last mile.

#10YearsOfUPI is therefore not merely a celebration of an app. It is a celebration of public digital infrastructure, institutional trust and inclusion by design. 🇮🇳

His story has sparked conversations about property rights, demolition procedures, due process and accountability in Abuja.

text:
#SupremeCourt Quashes #FIRs Against Student #Protesters Across #India

The Supreme Court has ordered the closure of FIRs registered across the country in connection with student protests held between July 20 and July 25.

A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana directed that the FIRs should not be pursued or investigated and must be treated as closed for all purposes.

The Court also specifically quashed FIRs identified in applications filed by the Centre through Delhi Police, as well as Bihar, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Assam. Although only these authorities approached the Court, the order has been extended pan-India.

The bench said the decision was taken keeping in mind the future of students who had participated in the protests bona fide.

The Court further directed that no State or Union Territory shall register any fresh FIR in connection with protest incidents that took place between July 20 and July 25.

However, an exception has been made for 2,873 individuals who were present at the Jantar Mantar protests and are alleged to have serious criminal antecedents. The Delhi Police has been permitted to proceed against them.

The Supreme Court invoked its special powers under Article 142 of the Constitution while passing the order. The bench clarified that the decision has been taken in view of the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and shall not be treated as a precedent.

The Court also recorded the Solicitor General’s assurance that the Centre will formulate, within three months, a policy for compensation to the families of students who died by suicide following the cancellation of NEET-UG 2026.

Following the government’s assurances and the Court’s order, CJP Co-Convener Saurav Das announced in court that the organisation was withdrawing its planned September 5 protest march in Delhi.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the Court that the applications were filed in accordance with assurances given by the Central Government on July 25 to CJP leaders that cases against protesters would be withdrawn and no fresh FIRs would be registered over the same incidents.

The Supreme Court had, during its August 18 hearing, indicated that it was inclined to use Article 142 to bring an end to the FIRs, after legal complications were raised regarding the withdrawal of FIRs once they had been registered.

The latest order provides major relief to student protesters while allowing authorities to continue proceedings against individuals with serious criminal backgrounds.

The running record of Trump 2.0 that America cannot afford to forget.

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Special thanks to Sr. Adv. Makarand D. Adkar Ji (@AdkarMakarand) for his guidance and support, and to the legal team for their efforts.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

SC Senior Advocate Mahesh Jethmalani Decodes The Legal Reality Of Faction Mergers

Senior Supreme Court advocate Mahesh Jethmalani clarified that the rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs who moved to merge with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) are legally protected under the anti-defection law, provided they meet the two-thirds threshold. He explained that a merger backed by two-thirds of the legislature party provides a "safe harbour" from parliamentary disqualification under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

Under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule, a breakaway faction is legally immune to disqualification if at least two-thirds of the members of the Legislature Party agree to merge with another political entity. With 20 rebel MPs splitting from TMC's 29-member lower house strength, they satisfy this legal benchmark.

Jethmalani explicitly ruled out any "dual membership" or subsequent claims to the original party. Once a faction chooses to merge with a new or existing entity like the NCPI, they entirely forfeit their right to claim the original TMC identity, name, or party symbol.

He noted a critical distinction between the current TMC crisis and the 2022 Shiv Sena split. In the Shiv Sena and NCP (Ajit Pawar) episodes, rival factions battled internally to claim they were the "real" original party. In contrast, the TMC rebels are actively executing a legal merger into a completely different registered political party, meaning they cannot double-back to claim the TMC brand.

Jethmalani dismissed political criticisms regarding the choice of the merging entity, stating there is nothing unconstitutional about merging with any registered political party, regardless of its size, optics, or lack of significant electoral footprint.

He observed that the current anti-defection framework inadvertently facilitates mass group defections via mergers while restricting individual floor-crossing, ultimately shifting political battles into lengthy judicial overhauls.

The worst industrial disaster in human history was caused by water getting into a tank.

Not sabotage, not an explosion, not fire. Water.

Here is what happened, and why the site is still killing people 42 years later.

The Union Carbide plant in Bhopal made a pesticide. To make it, they stored a chemical called methyl isocyanate, or MIC. It is the smallest and most toxic of its whole chemical family.

MIC has one property that makes it terrifying to store. It reacts violently with water.

Not slowly. The reaction generates its own heat, which speeds up the reaction, which generates more heat. Once it starts, it feeds itself.

On the night of 2nd December 1984, water entered storage tank 610.

The temperature inside began climbing. The pressure went with it. At around 11 at night, an operator noticed a small leak and rising pressure. Over the next 2 hours it ran away completely.

The plant had 6 safety systems designed for exactly this. A refrigeration unit to keep the MIC cold. A scrubber to neutralise escaping gas. A flare tower to burn it off. Others.

None of the 6 were working that night.

At about 1 in the morning a safety valve gave way and the gas went into the air over a sleeping city of roughly a million people.

Estimates of how much escaped range from about 27 to 45 tonnes.

Now the part that explains the death toll.

MIC attacks the lungs. It causes pulmonary edema, which means the lungs fill with fluid. People did not die of poisoning in the way most people imagine. They drowned, on dry land, in their own bodies.

There was no antidote. Doctors were initially told to treat it as cyanide poisoning and gave sodium thiosulfate. That was based on a wrong assumption about the chemical.

Around 40% of the women who were pregnant that night lost their pregnancies.

Immediate deaths are estimated between 3,000 and 8,000. Total deaths attributed to the exposure since then range from 15,000 to 25,000, depending on the source. Around half a million people were exposed.

Many survivors received compensation amounting to a few hundred dollars each.

Here is the part almost nobody outside Bhopal knows.

The factory was never cleaned up.

The waste pits and evaporation ponds on that site were never properly lined. They are still there. Chemicals have been leaching into the soil and the groundwater for 4 decades, and studies and court filings confirm the contamination has spread well beyond the factory walls.

People living around that site have been drinking that water.

In a recent operation, Indian authorities moved 337 tonnes of sealed waste to an incinerator. Campaigners pointed out that this material had already been packed in leak proof drums and sitting in a warehouse since 2005, and that it amounts to less than 1% of the estimated 1 million tonnes of contaminated material still on that land.

Union Carbide was acquired by Dow Chemical in 2001. Dow has consistently maintained that the liabilities were settled and that it is not responsible for the site.

So the gas killed people in 1984, and the ground has been killing them ever since.

Children have been born in those neighbourhoods, decades after the night itself, to parents who were not born in 1984 either.

The lesson is not about India. Every country has tanks like that one, and every one of them is safe only for as long as somebody keeps the cooling on and the scrubbers working.

Bhopal was not a freak event.

It was 6 safety systems switched off at the same time, in a plant nobody was watching.

WHEN CHILDREN NEED TO WADE THROUGH FLOODWATER TO REACH SCHOOL, CALL IT WHAT IT IS: ADMINISTRATIVE FAILURE

The image of children making their way through floodwater to reach school is not a symbol of “development”. It is a warning about the most basic responsibility of a government: keeping citizens, especially children, safe.

Prayagraj has faced severe waterlogging after days of heavy rain. Roads and low-lying areas were submerged, drains overflowed, and student accommodation was affected. The crisis became serious enough for the Allahabad High Court to take suo motu cognisance, summon senior officials and question why preventive measures had not been taken in advance. 

The Court subsequently directed authorities to deploy sufficient pumps and clear affected low-lying areas within 24 hours. 

Schools themselves were forced to close because of the dangerous conditions, while waterlogging continued to affect educational institutions and students. At CMP Degree College, students and teachers protested after water remained for more than a week, with allegations that overflowing drains and sewage were feeding into the campus. 

Yes, extraordinary rainfall can overwhelm any city. But that cannot become a permanent excuse for predictable, recurring failures of drainage and urban planning.

A government is not judged only by flyovers, highways, statues or slogans.

It is judged by whether a child can walk to school without having to cross filthy floodwater.

Children deserve safe roads, functioning drainage and dignity — not speeches about development.

USCIRF Commissioner Asif Mahmood wants "dialogue" with RSS when he has lost the debate on FACTS. 

THIS IS AN EXHAUSTIVE LINE-BY-LINE 7-PT TAKEDOWN OF HIS USCIRF REPORT ON RSS, MODI & INDIA.

1. RSS “SUBGROUPS” & VIOLENCE

MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF CONFLATION:
“Members of RSS subgroups have perpetrated violent attacks against religious minorities, including Christians, Dalits, Muslims, and Sikhs.”

WHY IT'S A DOUBLE STANDARD:
USCIRF says “members of RSS subgroups”, not that the RSS ordered, funded or organised these attacks. If the conduct of a member or affiliate automatically establishes the culpability of the parent organisation, then should the Cong party be held institutionally responsible for 1984 anti-Sikh riots where Cong leaders were convicted?

2. “HINDUTVA INHERENTLY DISCRIMINATES”
MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“The BJP has enforced policies that closely align with the RSS' Hindutva ideology, inherently discriminating against religious minority communities.”

WHY IT'S A SWEEPING STATEMENT WITHOUT EVIDENCE:
“Inherently discriminating” is a conclusion. Where has USCIRF identified specific discriminatory provisions. Infact, under BJP rule in Karnataka, when backward-class categories were reorganised in 2023, Christians and Jains remained eligible for reservation under Category 2D

3. “RSS SEEKS TO EXCLUDE NON-HINDUS”

UNSUBSTANTIATED USCIRF ACCUSATION:
The RSS promotes a Hindu 'Rastra' that excludes Muslims, Christians, Jews, Buddhists, Parsis and other religious communities.

WHY IT'S TOO BROAD:
Where is the RSS resolution saying “Muslims cannot be citizens,” “Christians cannot hold office,” or “non-Hindus must lose constitutional rights”? In fact RSS engages minorities through Muslim Rashtriya Manch.

4. CAA = ANTI-MUSLIM CITIZENSHIP LAW

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
The government has discriminated against Muslims through the Citizenship Amendment Act.

WHY ITS FACTUALLY WRONG:
The CAA creates an accelerated citizenship route for specified persecuted minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. It does not contain a provision stripping an INDIAN Muslim of existing CITIZENSHIP. In any case the CAA draws upon the logic of U.S. laws like the Lautenberg-Specter Amendment.

5. NRC “FORCIBLY EXPELLED MUSLIM CITIZENS”

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“Authorities have also forcefully expelled Muslim citizens in Assam under the National Register of Citizens (NRC) and Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA).”

WHY IT'S FACTUALLY WRONG:
The Assam NRC was published in 2019, but the legal process has not been operationalised to the point USCIRF's language suggests. The Gauhati High Court has recorded that the final NRC has not been notified in the Official Gazette, has not been given effect by the Government of India, and rejection slips have not been issued.

6. FCRA = THREAT TO FAITH-BASED ORGANISATIONS

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“Pending amendments to the FCRA [are] threatening the ability of faith-based organizations to continue their operations in the country.”

WHY IT'S MISLEADING:
FCRA regulates foreign contributions, not religious belief or the right to practise religion. Faith-based organisations can operate in India; the question is whether and under what conditions they can receive foreign funding. The United States itself has FARA, which regulates certain activities undertaken on behalf of foreign principals. If the U.S. can, why can't India?

7. UMAR KHALID = PERSECUTED FOR BEING MUSLIM

MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF CONFLATION:
“Religious minorities—like Umar Khalid, who has been detained since 2020 for leading peaceful protests opposing the religiously discriminatory CAA—often spend years in jail without a trial.”
WHY IT'S SLANDER:
USCIRF presents Khalid's detention as though he were imprisoned for opposing the CAA.
But SC'S Jan 2026 order records the prosecution material alleging that Khalid played a “central and formative role” in the violence and mobilisation.

When the price of a token falls, people do not pocket the savings and use the same amount of intelligence. They spend the surplus on more steps, longer context, extra retries, and jobs that were not worth running at the old price. That is why a collapse in cost per token does not shrink compute demand(like many AI Bears claimed). It multiplies it. A cheap token makes it rational to let an agent reread the repo, call tools, criticize its own draft, and try again, which is the same request a person used to make in one shot, only stretched across ten to fifty model turns. Each of those turns still needs accelerators spinning, memory bandwidth, and power, so the bill per useful outcome can drop while the machines required to deliver it rise. Jevons shows up here in the simplest form: inference got hundreds of times cheaper over a few years, token volume filled the gap, and agents turned that volume into a loop instead of a chat. The 10–50× demand for CPU is not a claim that chips got worse. It is the workload getting thicker because the unit of thought got cheap enough to waste on purpose.

Global Token consumption did not “jump overnight” in February 2026, but that month is the clearest inflection in who is burning the tokens: agents overtook humans on the best public telemetry, and global throughput kept compounding from an already-high base. 

That is +57% in the six months after mid January, or roughly +35% in the first quarter after the Feb inflection, then slower. On the chart, the solid floor is still only ~40–50 T through most of 2025, then steps up hard in late 2025 (China national series entering the ledger: 100 T by Dec 2025, 140 T by Mar 2026) and climbs from ~170 T around Feb ’26 toward ~300 T by June. 

Where Agentic AI actually shows up:

The sharpest agent specific series is OpenRouter (developer/API router, open-weight and tool heavy, not the whole market). Multiple write ups of OpenRouter / a16z data converge on the same story:
~Around 1–6 February 2026, agentic traffic crossed human traffic on the platform.
~Agentic tokens then went from ~0.51 T to ~7.3 T (14×) by mid-August.
~Human tokens grew only ~2.8× over the same window (to ~1.4–1.5 T).
~Agents therefore sit at ~5× human volume on that slice.

That is the operational meaning of “took the main stage.” Humans still ask questions, agents loop: plan → retrieve → tool call → critic → retry, often for hours. OpenRouter also reports tool call rates on some traffic rising from <5% to >25% over ~12 months, and 50%+ of output tokens as internal reasoning in places. Chinese coding/agent models (MiniMax, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek) took a large share of that February surge.

Agents inflate token counts so violently because they do not use a model the way a person does. A human asks a question, gets an answer, and stops. An agent treats that same model as a worker that has to keep going: break the job into steps, pull files or search results, call tools, check whether the result is any good, and try again if it is not. Each of those loops sends the model more text than the last one. The system prompt, the repo, the ticket, the docs, and the running scratchpad all come back again. That is why a task that looks like “fix this bug” can burn hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens while a normal chat uses a few thousand.

The expensive part is usually the input, not the clever paragraph at the end. The model has to reread a large context on every turn even when most of that context has not changed. Caching takes some of the sting out of the bill on instrumented traffic something like seventy to eighty-five percent of agent tokens are repeated prompts billed at a discount but the raw meter still spins. Research on agentic coding makes the gap concrete: those workloads can consume on the order of a thousand times more tokens than ordinary chat and several thousand times more than a single shot reasoning question. Two runs of the same ticket can also differ by an order of magnitude, because the agent wanders, retries, or over explains. Goldman’s shorthand is the same idea in plainer clothes, an agent is a chatbot request blown up ten to fifty times.

That is the February 2026 story underneath the global chart. The planet’s estimated throughput did not suddenly multiply by fourteen. It climbed from roughly two hundred thirty trillion tokens a day in mid January to about three hundred sixty by mid July. What changed composition was who was doing the consuming. On OpenRouter, the slice of the market where developers actually wire models to tools, agents crossed humans around the first week of February and then ran away with the graph: about fourteen times more agent tokens by August, against less than three times growth for people. Agents there now use several times as many tokens as humans. That platform is not the whole world Google’s product surfaces and China’s national totals still dominate the big index but it is the cleanest public picture of the new customer. The customer is no longer only a person typing. It is software that keeps the model on the clock.

China went from almost nothing in early 2024 to an official floor around one hundred forty trillion a day by spring 2026, with other Chinese reports implying the true number may already be higher. Google disclosed on the order of one hundred five trillion a day across first party and partner surfaces. OpenAI and Anthropic have to be inferred from APIs, revenue, and cost, so they sit in wider bands of tens of trillions each. Fireworks and similar hosts add another large pile of open-model serving. 

Costs per token have collapsed for years, and usage has filled every gap that created. Agents are simply the next intensity step: more tokens per useful outcome, not just more people chatting. If the longer forecasts that pin a twenty four times jump by 2030 on agentic demand are even roughly right, the chart you are looking at is the start of that shift, not the peak of it.

@AMD  is winning the unexpected race of 2026, and it is not the GPU race everyone spent two years staring at. Dr. Lisa Su is selling every high core EPYC it can build, raising its own server CPU revenue guide at rates that used to belong to accelerators, and sitting on roughly half of x86 server processor dollars even though it still ships fewer chips than Intel. In the first quarter AMD reached a record 46.2 percent of server CPU revenue with about a third of units; by the second quarter its adjusted EPYC versus Xeon unit share was near 46 percent as well. That combination, premium chips plus rising volume, is why the firm now expects server CPU revenue to grow more than 80 percent year over year in the second half of 2026 and more than 70 percent in 2027, and why it doubled its view of the market itself from an 18 percent CAGR to more than 35 percent, pointing at a $220 billion plus TAM by 2030. The driver is Agentic AI, and AMD already has the densest shipping product for the jobs those agents actually do.

The industry spent the first wave of generative AI treating the CPU as furniture. Training and token generation live on GPUs. Then models started acting: spawning sub agents, calling APIs, writing files, installing packages, compiling code, checking policy, and stuffing tool results back into a context that can run to hundreds of thousands or even a million tokens. That loop is not matrix math. Intel’s Souvik Kundu has said many stages of an agentic task are inherently CPU jobs: parse the output, pick a tool, make the call or run the code, collect the result, feed it back. AMD’s Madhu Rangarajan has gone further in public comments around the same research wave, arguing that in realistic pipelines most stages run entirely on the CPU. The GPU still does inference. Everything around it, the harness, the sandbox, the tokenizer, the guardrails, the enterprise services the agent is allowed to touch, is general purpose compute. That is why hyperscalers and AI Labs are scaling toward 1-2 CPU : 1 GPU.

You can see the strain in the cloud before you see it in a slide deck. AWS told internal engineers to stop wasting CPU cycles after wait times for CPU capacity stretched from hours to days. That is the world’s largest cloud operator treating spare EPYC and Graviton inventory like a scarce resource, not leftover capacity. Distributors report Intel fulfilling only about 40 percent of yearly server CPU backlog in places, with lead times measured in months. Some server CPU prices have jumped more than 40 percent in under a year. Intel has redirected older node wafer starts toward servers and industrial parts, which is another way of saying the money moved. Lip-Bu Tan has described CEOs calling him for more CPUs. When both the volume leader and the share gainer are sold out, the bottleneck is real.

The technical bottleneck is more specific than “agents use computers.” Tokenization is a good example. Converting text into token IDs is branchy, data dependent string work. On a short chat prompt it is cheap. On an agent that keeps appending tool results and then re-tokenizes a 100,000 token running sequence, it is not. Georgia Tech work associated with Euijun Chung found that too few CPU cores leave GPUs idle waiting for the next dispatch, and that adding cores can cut time to first token by roughly 1.5x to 7x on long sequences. Kundu’s group, also tied to Georgia Tech and Intel, showed that GPUs and CPUs take turns sitting idle in agentic pipelines and that better scheduling can cut end to end latency by up to about 1.8x under load. Safety checks often stay on the CPU too, because they are small, rule heavy, and latency sensitive. None of that is a GPU’s favorite job. All of it scales with the number of agents, and agents scale with each other.

This is where AMD’s product shape matches the workload. Fifth generation EPYC Turin already goes to 192 cores. Sixth generation Venice, ramping on TSMC 2 nm, is aimed at 256 cores and 512 threads, with AMD talking about much higher memory bandwidth per socket and a portfolio split on purpose: dense parts for agent sandboxes, high frequency parts to keep GPUs fed as host nodes, and general purpose SKUs for the databases and services agents call. AMD’s own rack modeling current Turin configuration can put more than 27,000 cores in a liquid-cooled rack class and that Venice stretches that toward 36,000-81,000, with modeled 100 kW rack throughput well ahead of Intel’s Granite Rapids and Nvidia’s 88 core Vera baseline. Agentic fleets care about agents per watt, per dollar, and per rack, plus the boring fact that most enterprise tools still speak x86. AMD has been selling that combination into cloud instances that grew about 50 percent to more than 1,600 publicly listed EPYC shapes. Venice demand, Su has said, is stronger than for any prior generation.

$NVDA  Jensen Huang’s line is that agents will be the largest users of computing. If Vera stays tied to Rubin racks and a few hyperscalers, it is a specialist. If it leaks into general CPU servers, AMD’s density argument has to keep winning on software compatibility and cores per rack, not just slides. Arm designs from AWS Graviton5, Qualcomm, and others are also being pitched as orchestration silicon. The field is getting crowded because the money moved.

The uncomfortable part is that a CPU crunch does not stay in the data center. When wafer starts, substrates, and packaging follow server ASPs, client CPUs get rationed, prices rise, and PC makers feel it. Analysts already talk about the shortage trickling into consumer channels the way GPU and HBM shortages did. AMD is following the money too; that is what a winner does. The risk for buyers is simple. Agentic systems multiply work at machine speed. Every extra tool call is more tokenization, more Python, more syscalls, more policy checks. Software can hide some of that with smarter scheduling and incremental tokenizers. It cannot repeal the need for cores, memory bandwidth, and I/O sitting next to the GPU.

Dr. Lisa Su’s EPYC bet only looks obvious now. For years it meant shipping more cores, more memory bandwidth, and a cleaner chiplet design while the industry stared at GPUs. The real wager was simpler than a forecast about agents: the data center would still need a fast, dense, x86 processor to run other people’s software. That is the work agents do once they leave the GPU and start calling tools, compiling code, hitting databases, re-tokenizing long context, and enforcing policy. Turin at 192 cores and Venice aimed at 256 were not built for a keynote slogan. They were built for messy concurrent jobs, and that is suddenly the scarce layer in AI infrastructure.

The market is paying her back in the dull numbers. AMD now takes close to half of x86 server processor revenue while still shipping fewer units than Intel, cloud catalogs keep adding EPYC instances, and Dr. Su can guide server CPU growth above 80 percent in the second half of 2026 because customers raised their own CPU plans first. EPYC is already the high volume way to run the non-GPU half of an agent fleet without a software rewrite. She did not need to predict agentic AI in 2017. She needed to keep the unglamorous compute layer excellent until the next wave of software ran into it. It did.

🔥Noise ≠ nihilism; patriotism ≠ persecution. India’s constitutional engine still forges truthful speech + plural nation—by design, doctrine, and delivery. Watch the evidence. #UPSC #GS2 #GS4 #PSIR ⚖️🇮🇳

A. “Collapse of sincerity” vs “Working constitutional speech-market” — juxtaposed refutation

Claim (Mehta): algorithms monetise performance; sincerity is dead.

Counter (law-anchored): India’s system builds, protects, and disciplines truthful communication.

Free speech spine intact: Art.19(1)(a); limits only under Art.19(2)—sovereignty, integrity (via 16th Amend., 1963), public order, decency, contempt, defamation, incitement.

Shreya Singhal (2015): struck 66A IT Act; mandated narrow tests (“incitement”, “tendency to create”). Sincerity space preserved.

Right to know fuels deliberation: PUCL v. Union (2003) & ADR (2002)—candidate disclosures as Art.19(1)(a); RTI Act 2005 operationalises truth access, not performance.

State coercion checked: Anuradha Bhasin (2020)—internet restrictions must be proportional, reasoned, reviewable. Kaushal Kishor (2023)—remedies exist for ministerial speech harm; no blanket gag on political speech.

Harmful speech contained, not chilled: Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation to protect Art.21 reputation; Amish Devgan (2020) clarified hate-speech thresholds—ethics by law, not by vibe.

Platform due-diligence (not censorship): IT (Intermediary Guidelines & Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021—grievance officers, 36-hr takedown on court/LEA orders, traceability for heinous crimes; 69A IT Act blocking only via speaking orders + review (per Shreya Singhal).

Election truth-checks: Model Code of Conduct, cVIGIL, paid-news rules; ECI + SVEEP strengthen voter information.

Civic transparency expanding: Open Government Data, Proactive RTI (s.4), Social Audit (MNREGA/SSA rules)—institutionalise fact visibility.

Bottom line: The architecture prizes sincerity by rights (19(1)(a)), guardrails (19(2)), remedies (courts/RTI/ECI). The market is noisy; the constitution makes it corrigible.

Editorial: “Unkind cuts” — ECI’s voter deletions

Core Idea

Editorial questions the large-scale deletion of voters during the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Telangana and Karnataka.

1. Scale of deletions

Around 22% voters in Telangana and 19.5% in Karnataka were reportedly deleted.

Bengaluru saw some constituencies losing more than half their electors.

Hyderabad had several constituencies with over 40% deletions.

Such massive deletions cannot simply be dismissed as routine cleaning of electoral rolls.

2. Why is it problematic?

If voters have merely migrated within the same State, their names should be shifted rather than deleted.

The editorial argues that available survey and population data do not sufficiently justify such large reductions.

Therefore, transparency + verification become essential.

3. Democratic concern

The right to vote is central to universal adult franchise.
Wrongful deletion can lead to disenfranchisement—a citizen being effectively excluded from democratic participation.

4. Institutional accountability

ECI has reportedly not provided adequate elector-to-population ratios and detailed deletion data.

Karnataka’s deletion lists lacked easily verifiable details such as old booth numbers, making verification difficult.

Political parties and citizens also need to actively file objections.

5. Larger lesson

Electoral-roll revision is necessary to remove dead, duplicate or shifted voters, but the process must never sacrifice legitimate voters.

Way Forward:
Transparency → searchable deletion lists → door-to-door verification → easy claims & objections → independent audit → timely restoration of wrongly deleted names.
