Michael John-Hopkins published a piece in Opinio Juris this week arguing that platforms have an obligation to manage the information environment during elections, not just pull specific pieces of foreign-origin content after the fact. The framing is "noise reduction" as a defensive posture. Read it as a signal about where the legal and regulatory conversation is heading, because that's what it is.

The operational logic behind his argument is worth sitting with. Foreign influence operations, the documented ones, don't depend on any single piece of content succeeding. They depend on volume, timing, and platform architecture doing the amplification work for them. The GRU's 2016 operation, the Internet Research Agency's content farms, the Iranian personas caught running coordinated inauthentic behavior in 2020, none of them needed to convince a majority of anyone. They needed to flood specific moments, debates, counting windows, candidate announcement cycles, with enough noise to degrade the signal. Platforms rewarding emotional provocation handled the rest.

John-Hopkins's intervention is that removal-after-detection is structurally too slow for this threat model. By the time a piece of content is attributed, reviewed, and removed, it's already done its work. The cycle from posting to viral spread to mainstream pickup now routinely runs faster than any moderation queue. His proposed alternative is governance at the environment level: reducing algorithmic amplification during high-stakes windows rather than chasing individual posts.

This is where the trajectory gets interesting. He's not the first to make this argument. Renee DiResta and the Stanford Internet Observatory crowd have been documenting the amplification problem for years. But a formal legal framing in Opinio Juris, routed through international law and democratic obligation, signals something: this argument is moving from the security research community into the legal and regulatory pipeline. That's a different kind of momentum.

What to watch on the regulatory side: the European Union's Digital Services Act already has hooks for this. It requires very large online platforms to assess and mitigate "systemic risks" to electoral processes, and the European Commission has been explicit that algorithmic amplification of foreign interference content is one such risk. The Commission's preliminary findings on X after Elon Musk's reinstatement of suspended accounts, and the ongoing DSA proceeding against the platform, sit directly on this question. The EU is not waiting for a theoretical framework. They're already building enforcement posture around it.

In the United States the legal terrain is messier. X Corp. v. Bonta, the challenge to California's content moderation disclosure law, is working through the courts. The New York Stop Hiding Hate Act litigation John-Hopkins mentions directly raised First Amendment questions about mandated platform transparency. The current composition of the Supreme Court is not hospitable to arguments that platforms can be compelled by government to structure their information environments in particular ways, even defensive ones. That's a genuine constraint. John-Hopkins acknowledges it and essentially argues that disclosure and transparency requirements are the legally sustainable pathway in the American context. Require platforms to show their work on algorithmic amplification rather than mandate specific architectural changes. That's probably correct as a constitutional matter, and it's also a narrower intervention than what the threat model actually calls for.

Here's what the trajectory looks like on the adversary side. Russia, Iran, and China all learned from 2016 and 2020. The IRA operation was effective partly because it was crude enough that human analysts could find it once they were looking. The operations documented since then are more distributed, more reliant on domestic amplification nodes, more careful about metadata hygiene. The 2024 cycle saw STORM-1516, the Russian operation pushing fabricated video content, explicitly time its releases to coincide with news cycles, not because the content was more convincing but because the news cycle created the noise cover. The playbook is already adapted to a detection-and-removal defensive posture. It's built around making attribution slow and uncertain while the content circulates.

An environment-level defense, if it were actually implemented, would force a different adaptation. Reducing algorithmic amplification during debate windows or vote-counting periods doesn't require you to identify the foreign actor or prove attribution. It just reduces the operational leverage. Adversaries adapting to that would need either much larger genuine domestic networks to substitute for platform amplification, or different timing strategies, or content that spreads through channels less susceptible to platform-level governance. The first option is hard and expensive. The second and third are possible, and they're what defenders should be modeling now.

Specifically: if platforms began implementing even voluntary noise reduction during defined high-sensitivity windows, expect adversary operations to shift toward pre-election timing. Seeding content and narratives weeks before a critical window so that organic recirculation carries them through it. The GRU's "pre-loading" approach in European elections, where influence content was staged well ahead of voting day, is the template. The Macron leaks in 2017 dropped three days before the election, timed to sit at the edge of the blackout period under French law. That kind of timing is already part of the toolkit. It would become dominant.

For officials and election administrators: the John-Hopkins framing gives you a legal vocabulary that's been missing. The argument that platform environment governance is analogous to physical security measures protecting elections, not censorship of political speech, is useful in policy debates where "censorship" framing has dominated. Whether or not any specific legislative proposal survives First Amendment review, having a coherent legal theory matters for the regulatory conversation at the state level, in international forums, and in DSA compliance discussions if you're operating in Europe.

For voters: the operational implication of all this is that the moments you feel most overwhelmed by contradictory information, the hour after a debate, the first night of vote counting, the day a major candidate story breaks, are precisely the moments foreign operations are designed to target. That's not paranoia. It's documented pattern. Slowing down during those windows is more protective than any content filter.

One number that grounds this: the Stanford Internet Observatory's 2022 midterm review documented that coordinated inauthentic behavior spiked 300 percent in the 72 hours around Election Day compared to baseline. The content itself was less important than the timing. Platform architecture that reduced amplification during that specific window would have degraded the operation without identifying a single foreign account.

John-Hopkins's piece doesn't solve the First Amendment problem and doesn't tell platforms exactly how to implement noise reduction in practice. What it does is establish the legal and democratic theory clearly enough that regulators in jurisdictions with different constitutional frameworks, primarily the EU, have grounds to push harder on specific platform obligations. Watch the DSA enforcement track against X as the live version of this argument playing out. The Commission's ability to impose structural requirements on algorithmic amplification, including during elections, is legally grounded in a way the American framework currently isn't.

The piece is from Oxford Brookes, published in a respected international law forum, and it's going to get cited. That's the trajectory. Not a solved problem. A legitimized argument entering the regulatory pipeline on both sides of the Atlantic while adversaries who've already adapted to the old defensive model are running the next operation.

WHEN THE VOTE ITSELF IS TARGETED, DEMOCRACY IS UNDER ATTACK
This is not merely about BJP versus BJD.
It is about something much more fundamental: whether every Indian citizen has an equal right to exist on the electoral roll and participate in democracy.
An investigation by The Reporters’ Collective, published on August 30, 2026, reports that BJP booth-level agents submitted hundreds of Form 7 applications seeking deletion of Muslim voters in Bhadrak, Odisha. The investigation found evidence of digitally prepared forms, targeting across Muslim-dominated booths, and deletion requests concentrated exclusively on Muslim names. Booth-level officers interviewed by the publication said at least 30 booths were affected, with more than 100 deletion requests reported at some booths.
The most disturbing question, however, is not simply who filed the forms.
It is what the state did after receiving complaints.
According to the investigation, voters and opposition representatives complained about the alleged bogus deletions. Yet instead of immediately investigating those responsible, district officials directed booth-level officers to reverify the very voters who had been targeted. One head BLO reportedly found that the flagged Muslim voters under his supervision were legitimate.
That raises a fundamental democratic principle:
A voter should not have to prove their right to vote because someone has allegedly attempted to erase them from the electoral roll.
If a Form 7 application contains knowingly false information, the law must be applied to the person making the false claim—not transformed into a burden placed upon the targeted citizen.
And if political workers systematically identify citizens by religion and attempt to remove them from the electorate, the issue goes far beyond partisan politics.
It becomes a question of equal citizenship.
India's Constitution does not recognise first-class and second-class voters.
It does not say that a Hindu vote is more legitimate than a Muslim vote, or that a Muslim citizen must repeatedly prove their belonging before exercising a constitutional democratic right.
One citizen. One vote. Equal dignity. Equal protection.
That principle must survive regardless of which party benefits electorally.
If these allegations are false, there should be a transparent investigation that establishes that fact.
If they are true, those responsible must face the full consequences of the law.
And if officials ignored credible evidence of coordinated voter suppression, their conduct too deserves scrutiny.
Because democracy is not merely the act of counting votes on election day.
Democracy begins with ensuring that every eligible citizen is still allowed to have a vote to count.
The Election Commission must therefore provide a transparent, booth-wise account of the Form 7 objections, independently investigate allegations of coordinated targeting, protect every legitimate voter from wrongful deletion, and prosecute deliberate false filings wherever the evidence establishes criminal wrongdoing.
The standard cannot be BJP, BJD, Congress, Muslim or Hindu.
The standard must be:
TRUTH. EQUALITY. CONSTITUTIONAL MORALITY. AND THE RIGHT OF EVERY CITIZEN TO BE HEARD.
Anything less is not electoral integrity.
It is the erosion of democracy itself.
Source: The Reporters’ Collective — investigation by Ayushi Kar, edited by Nitin Sethi.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Through the ongoing protests and movements in India, the exploitation and irregularities perpetrated by the ruling BJP and its administration are no longer hidden. This is not an ordinary political conflict; it is a systematic attempt to destroy people's rights, freedom of expression, and democratic practices within the state framework.

Every step seems to be using state power as a weapon to suppress opponents. Labeling political rivals as "foreign agents," "anti-nationals," or "extremists," and then subjecting them to false cases, surveillance, and administrative harassment—these have become routine occurrences to serve a specific party's interests.

It is not just political opponents; ordinary citizens are also victims of this exploitation. Women, students, farmers, and even journalists participating in protests are facing brutality—police violence, arrests, and the burden of fabricated cases. Internet shutdowns, social media censorship, and pressure on independent media have turned India into what resembles an authoritarian state.

International human rights organizations have repeatedly highlighted these irregularities and exploitation, but the Indian government dismisses them as "internal matters." However, the reality is that these steps by the BJP government completely disregard democratic values and aim to bring the entire state machinery under one party's control.

Muslims, Dalits, and tribal communities are the most affected. Violence against them is increasing, they are being deprived of education and employment, and their religious-cultural identity is being questioned. This is not just a political conflict; this is a socio-cultural genocide-like situation targeting a community.

This situation is not just an internal matter of India; it is a matter of serious concern for Bangladesh and all neighboring countries. Because this instability and lawlessness in India can directly impact the geopolitical stability of South Asia. The effects of this exploitation and irregularities from across the border could spill over into our country, posing a major challenge for the future.

When Journalism Stops Asking Questions, Democracy Starts Losing Its Voice

“The biggest danger facing the media in India is that of selling out.” — Mrinal Pande

That is not merely a criticism of journalists. It is a warning about the health of Indian democracy.

In the Cine Ink – London Varta conversation, veteran journalist Mrinal Pande describes a media environment where the “price” being placed on journalists has become unprecedented. She also raises a deeper concern: when journalism begins behaving like a circus—performing, entertaining and avoiding serious questions—the public loses the institution that is supposed to hold power accountable. 

And the numbers make this concern harder to dismiss.

India ranks 157th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, down from 151st in 2025. Reporters Without Borders says press freedom in India is in crisis amid violence against journalists, concentrated media ownership and increasingly overt political alignment. 

But the real crisis is not simply a ranking.

It is what happens when journalists become more afraid of power than power is afraid of journalism.

A democracy cannot remain healthy if questioning a government, challenging an establishment, exposing institutional failures or defending dissent is treated as an act of hostility.

A government should be able to tolerate criticism.
A democracy must protect dissent.
And journalism must be able to ask uncomfortable questions.

When mainstream media repeatedly ignores serious allegations, while amplifying spectacle, outrage and political theatre, journalism gradually stops being a watchdog and becomes part of the machinery it was supposed to scrutinise.

That is when “selling out” becomes more dangerous than censorship.

Because censorship tells citizens that they are being silenced.

A compromised media can make citizens believe that nobody needs to speak.

The answer is not to demand that every journalist oppose the government. Journalism is not opposition politics.

The answer is much simpler—and much more radical:

Question everyone.
Investigate everyone.
Scrutinise everyone.
Protect dissent, even when you dislike the dissenter.

A journalist's loyalty should not belong to a political party, government, corporation or ideology.

It should belong to truth—and ultimately to the public.

The greatest danger to democracy may not be a journalist who asks a difficult question.

It may be an entire media ecosystem that has forgotten how.

Fine platforms.

Criticising a government, disagreeing with its decisions, questioning those in power, and political satire are fundamental to democratic discourse—not privileges granted by the government of the day.

If a post violates a legitimate law, explain why.
If it doesn't, why is it being blocked?

A democracy must protect citizens from unlawful speech without protecting governments from lawful criticism.

The ChatGPT integration for Apple Messages isn't installed or enabled by default. But privacy implications extend beyond Apple customers. Anyone messaging an Apple user who enables it is affected, including people using Android or GrapheneOS.

An Apple user must install the integration and give it access to Messages on their Mac. You can't know whether someone you communicated with in the past or will communicate with in the future has given ChatGPT access to your conversations.

Over 100 people across LinkedIn, X and Substack asked me how to disable it or protect their right to privacy. There’s nothing you can disable on your own device to stop someone else from giving ChatGPT access to your conversations.

You can't know which of your messages ChatGPT accessed through someone else, what information it extracted, what's retained or whether that data could later be obtained or misused.

Once OpenAI stores message content, law enforcement, intelligence agencies and governments can demand data that end to end encryption blocked Apple from turning over. 

The FBI has never been able to crack iMessage and failed to pressure Apple into giving them a backdoor. OpenAI has created another way to access everyone's messages.

End to end encryption is not broken, but its value is removed if everyone’s messages can be scanned and stored before they’re encrypted and after they’re decrypted.

Past conversations stay vulnerable because ChatGPT evaluates more than new texts. It accesses message history and attachments stored on Mac or synchronised through Messages in iCloud, analysing names, locations, and personal relationships.

Someone else can hand ChatGPT your past and future messages without your knowledge or consent.

Snowden revealed that mass surveillance didn’t require governments to intercept every private conversation themselves. Intelligence agencies obtained vast communications data through tech and telecom companies’ centralised infrastructure to search, analyse, and map connections at scale. Entire populations became searchable simply because their communications passed through entities subject to government access powers. 

His disclosures proved that infrastructure built for everyday communication turns into surveillance infrastructure once governments access the underlying data.

"When you say ‘I don’t care about the right to privacy because I have nothing to hide,’ that’s no different than saying ‘I don’t care about freedom of speech because I have nothing to say'".

"Simply because you are following the law, doesn’t mean that you’ll be exempt from governmental interference in your private life".

- Edward Snowden

What can you do?

Stop using the default Messages app on your iPhone, Android or @GrapheneOS device.

Ask people if they have given ChatGPT access to Apple Messages.

Don’t enable it. Respect other people’s right to privacy. Before my interview started with Fortune yesterday, the journalist asked if I was ok with her recording it with AI. I said yes because everything was on the record. But when we collaborate in the future, I might ask her not to. 

Context is everything.

For sensitive conversations, use Signal until prvc(.)app is publicly available through the launch of Mackie Mobile. That’s in the US, but it will be available via other partners outside the US. I’ll provide more information when I get it myself. 

Dislcaimer: I'm not part of the team. But I am working very closely with @_Johan_Mackie_ at the Mackie Mobile team to make mobile devices safer to use.

If you want a friendly way to ask friends and colleagues to tell you when they add AI to your private conversations, share this with them.

The implications are global because you don't need an Apple device, ChatGPT or an OpenAI account to be exposed.

Arguing that someone could take screenshots, share messages manually, or print them for law enforcement isn't a valid comparison. An individual choosing to disclose a conversation is fundamentally different from granting a third party ongoing access to private message histories involving everyone they contact.

💡 End to end encryption isn’t broken. But what’s the point of protecting messages in transit if a third party service can access them on a participant’s device before they’re sent or after they’re received, exposing those conversations to many of the same privacy risks that end to end encryption is supposed to prevent?

Messages app doesn't just support SMS, it supports iMessage and depending on the device and carrier, end to end encryption for RCS.

---

@TimSweeneyEpic is right to flag that my argument could be abused by Apple as evidence for its broader claim that opening its platforms to third party developers creates additional privacy and security risks. 

Apple already makes that argument around interoperability, so I want to be explicit: I strongly support Apple opening its platforms and oppose using privacy and security as a justification for anticompetitive restrictions. 

This is a unique case that requires a unique solution. It’s different even from highly intrusive integrations with operating systems or email because these are end to end encrypted conversations involving other people who reasonably believe their messages remain within that encrypted conversation. Perhaps not always, but sometimes.

Millions of people x sometimes = massive exposure.

In the Puttaswamy Judgment, the Supreme Court of India affirmed that the right to privacy is a fundamental right. The State can infringe this right only if the measure satisfies the following requirements:

- A valid law must exist to permit the state action.
- There must be a legitimate state aim for which the restriction on privacy is justified.
- The means adopted under the law must be proportional to the objective of the law.

A 2.6 million-view Instagram reel documenting the concerns of residents affected by a proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India without prior notice, a hearing, or a copy of the blocking order being provided to the journalists who made it. When the order was finally obtained through litigation, it referred to an entirely unrelated individual. IFF has now sought a review and restoration of the reel.
Read More: https://t.co/z4Ps7Umqrk

The blocking order itself raised serious concerns. It referred to a person named Mr. Vemireddy Prabhakar Reddy, who is entirely unknown to the journalists and has no connection whatsoever with the reel, which featured interviews with residents of Tarluvada village. The journalists were also never given an opportunity to respond or defend their reporting. (6/7)

IFF has now issued a legal notice seeking a periodic review of the blocking under the IT Rules, 2021, a proper hearing for the journalists, disclosure of the grounds for the restriction, and restoration of the reel. A factual ground report affecting freedom of speech and journalistic work cannot be restricted through an opaque process without procedural safeguards. (7/7)

text:
A Delhi High Court order has once again had to remind the Grievance Appellate Committee to follow the timeline already prescribed under the IT Rules, 2021. On 20 August 2026, the Court directed the GAC to decide the appeal of content creator Riya, whose Instagram account #riaspeaks has over five lakh followers, within 30 days. Her appeal had already been pending for more than 42 days. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/26gA6SeMe0

The GAC is particularly important because it is supposed to provide users with an appellate remedy against intermediary decisions, including arbitrary or permanent account bans. Yet when an appeal itself remains pending beyond the prescribed period, a creator can be left with no meaningful remedy except approaching a High Court. The burden then falls on users and the judiciary alike. (6/7)

IFF had earlier suggested increasing the number of GACs to deal with the growing volume of appeals and making GAC orders publicly accessible, given the quasi-adjudicatory nature of their work. Neither has happened. We are assisting Riya through the appeal process and will continue to monitor the matter. (7/7)
Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

Riya is an independent content creator whose Instagram account has built an audience of over five lakh followers through explainers on current affairs and public-interest issues. Her work has included analyses of the India–Pakistan hostilities, consumer rights, and the saline groundwater crisis in Maharashtra. For her, the account is also a livelihood built over years. (2/7)
